questions.prompt: Which bone forms the lateral part of the pectoral girdle and articulates with the head of the humerus?
Which of the following is NOT one of the eight carpal (wrist) bones?
Which bone is the longest bone in the body?
Which three bones fuse together to form each hip (coxal) bone?
A joint replacement that substitutes an artificial device for a damaged joint is called a(n):
Which two bones make up the pectoral girdle, and which of the two attaches directly to the axial skeleton?
questions.modelAnswer: The clavicle and the scapula. Only the clavicle attaches to the axial skeleton, at the sternoclavicular joint with the manubrium.

questions.prompt: Which forearm bone lies on the thumb side of the forearm in anatomical position?
questions.modelAnswer: The radius. The ulna is medial, on the little-finger side.

questions.prompt: The pectoral girdle attaches to the axial skeleton at only one joint (the sternoclavicular joint). How does this loose attachment contribute to the upper limb's wide range of motion?
questions.modelAnswer: The scapula is held mostly by muscles, not bone, so it can slide, rotate, and tilt on the rib cage. Combined with the shallow glenoid cavity, this lets the shoulder move through the widest range of any joint, at the cost of stability.

questions.prompt: What feature of the scapula articulates with the head of the humerus, and what feature articulates with the clavicle?
questions.modelAnswer: The glenoid cavity receives the head of the humerus; the acromion articulates with the clavicle.

questions.prompt: How many carpal bones are in each wrist, and how are they arranged?
questions.modelAnswer: Eight, in two rows of four. Proximal row (lateral to medial): scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.

questions.prompt: How many phalanges does the thumb have? How many does the pinky have?
questions.modelAnswer: The thumb has two (proximal and distal). The pinky and every other finger have three (proximal, middle, distal). 14 per hand.

questions.prompt: Why might a fracture of the scaphoid be more clinically significant than a fracture of one of the other carpal bones?
questions.modelAnswer: The scaphoid's blood supply enters at its distal end, so a fracture across the waist can cut off blood to the proximal fragment. It heals slowly and can die (avascular necrosis), leading to wrist arthritis. It is also the most commonly fractured carpal, from falls on an outstretched hand.

questions.prompt: Which structure forms the deep socket that receives the head of the femur?
questions.modelAnswer: The acetabulum, formed where the ilium, ischium, and pubis meet.

questions.prompt: Compare the pelvic girdle to the pectoral girdle. Which is built for mobility and which for stability, and how do their bony features reflect that?
questions.modelAnswer: The pectoral girdle is built for mobility: a shallow glenoid cavity and a single bony attachment to the axial skeleton (sternoclavicular joint). The pelvic girdle is built for stability: a deep acetabulum enclosing the femoral head and firm attachment to the sacrum at two sacroiliac joints plus the pubic symphysis.

questions.prompt: Which bony landmarks form the bumps you can feel on the inside and outside of your ankle, and which bone forms each?
questions.modelAnswer: Inside: the medial malleolus of the tibia. Outside: the lateral malleolus of the fibula.

questions.prompt: The fibula bears very little body weight, yet a fracture near the lateral malleolus can still be seriously disabling. Why?
questions.modelAnswer: The lateral malleolus forms the outer wall of the ankle mortise that holds the talus in place. If it breaks, the ankle joint loses its lateral stability and the talus can shift, making walking painful and unstable.

questions.prompt: Which tarsal bone articulates directly with the tibia and fibula to form the ankle joint?
questions.modelAnswer: The talus.

questions.prompt: Which tarsal bone forms the heel?
questions.modelAnswer: The calcaneus.

questions.prompt: Compare the bones of the foot to the bones of the hand. Which bones are analogous, and how do their proportions differ?
questions.modelAnswer: Tarsals correspond to carpals, metatarsals to metacarpals, and the toe phalanges to the finger phalanges. The foot has 7 tarsals to the hand's 8 carpals. The tarsals, especially the talus and calcaneus, are much larger for weight bearing, while the toe phalanges are short; the hand has long phalanges for grasping.

questions.prompt: A patient arrives after a fall with a suspected fracture of the 'greater trochanter.' Which bone and region does this refer to?
questions.modelAnswer: The femur, at the top of the thigh just below the hip joint; the greater trochanter is the lateral bump you can feel on the side of the hip.

questions.prompt: Which of the three joint replacements recreates a deep, stable ball-and-socket, and which components form the ball and the socket?
questions.modelAnswer: The hip: the femoral component (a ball on a stem in the femur) is the ball and the acetabular cup with its liner is the socket. The shoulder is also ball-and-socket but shallow; the knee is a hinge-like resurfacing.

questions.prompt: How does a reverse shoulder replacement swap the position of the ball and socket compared with the standard replacement?
questions.modelAnswer: In the standard design the ball is on the humerus and the socket on the scapula, like the natural joint. In the reverse design the ball is fixed to the glenoid of the scapula and the socket is on the humeral stem, which lets the deltoid raise the arm when the rotator cuff is torn.

questions.prompt: What are osteophytes, and when do they appear in osteoarthritis?
questions.modelAnswer: Bone spurs: bony outgrowths at the joint margins. They appear once cartilage has worn enough for bone to bear load, typically from the moderate stage onward, and are prominent in advanced disease.

questions.prompt: Describe two changes in advanced osteoarthritis and explain how each could make a joint replacement necessary.
questions.modelAnswer: Articular cartilage is worn away so bone grinds on bone, causing pain and loss of motion; and osteophytes plus thickened, deformed bone surfaces distort the joint. A replacement resurfaces both bone ends with smooth artificial components to restore pain-free movement.

questions.prompt: Is the ulna the medial or lateral bone of the forearm? Is the tibia the medial or lateral bone of the leg?
questions.modelAnswer: The ulna is medial (little-finger side). The tibia is medial (big-toe side).

questions.prompt: List the bone groups of the appendicular skeleton with counts.
questions.modelAnswer: Pectoral girdle: 2 clavicles, 2 scapulae. Upper limbs: 2 humeri, 2 radii, 2 ulnae, 16 carpals, 10 metacarpals, 28 phalanges. Pelvic girdle: 2 hip bones. Lower limbs: 2 femora, 2 patellae, 2 tibiae, 2 fibulae, 14 tarsals, 10 metatarsals, 28 phalanges. 126 bones total.
